Simon Goulart
sē-mohn' goo-lar'
n. (Simon Goulart, 1543–1628, Geneva pastor, editor and translator)
Hebrew Shimon, hearing, through Greek Simon; French Goulart, a Senlis family name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Simon Goulart pastored in Geneva for more than fifty years and produced an output that is hard to credit: translations from Latin and Greek, editions of the Fathers and of the Reformers, commentaries, histories of the French wars, collections of martyr accounts, and the moderating of the Company of Pastors after Beza died. He wrote and edited because the presses of Geneva were the arsenal of the French Reformed churches, and a church under persecution needs books more than it needs committees. Not much of it is read now, and almost none of it was original; that was the point. A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver (Pro 25:11), and Goulart spent a long life setting other men's words in silver so that the French churches could have them.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines editor as one who prepares a work for publication, and translate as to interpret in another language.

expand to see more

ED'ITOR, n. A publisher; particularly, a person who superintends an impression of a book; one who revises and prepares a work for publication.

TRANSLA'TE, v.t. To interpret; to render into another language; to express the sense of one language in the words of another.

PRESS, n. A machine for printing; called a printing-press.

MAR'TYROLOGY, n. A history or account of martyrs with their sufferings.

Modern Corruption

Fifty years in a Geneva pulpit and an output of translations, editions and histories.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the premium the modern world puts on originality, which leaves the translator, editor and compiler looking like a man who had no ideas of his own. Goulart had plenty and spent them on other men's books, because a persecuted church in France needed Augustine, Calvin and the martyr accounts in print and in French more than it needed his opinions.

The principle to recover is that the written record is for the use of those who come after, and comfort is one of its stated purposes. “For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope” (Rom 15:4). The craftsman's own standard is Solomon's: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver” (Pro 25:11).
